To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the association between cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), alcohol intake and metabolic syndrome (MS) was not modified by age, sex, race, or BMI.

1) a higher level of cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is associated with a lower risk of developing metabolic syndrome in men and 2) a moderate to high level of alcohol consumption is associated with a higher risk of developing metabolic syndromes in men.

(i) the association between alcohol consumption and metabolic syndrome is U-shaped; (ii) the lowest risk is observed at 1-2 drinks/day; and (iii) the risk increases at higher levels of alcohol intake.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of physical activity and fitness on the incidence of metabolic syndrome and its component disorders in men.
the effects of alcohol consumption on the development of metabolic syndrome (MS) in men and women.
the relationship between cardiorespiratory fitness and metabolic syndrome incidence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to determine if cardiorespiratory fitness and alcohol intake are associated with metabolic syndrome.
cardiorespiratory fitness is associated with reduced risk for the development of the Metabolic Syndrome, independent of alcohol intake and vice versa.
the association between alcohol consumption and the incidence of metabolic syndrome is not consistent and is likely to depend on the type of beverage consumed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metabolic syndrome is associated with a reduced level of physical fitness.

a high cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) level is associated with a decreased risk for metabolic syndrome (MetS) incidence, and alcohol consumption is associated with a lower risk of developing MetS in men with high CRF levels.
the results from the current study suggest that cardiorespiratory fitness and alcohol consumption may be independently associated with metabolic syndrome risk in men.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the association between cardiorespiratory fitness and metabolic syndrome incidence was modified by alcohol intake in men.
cardiorespiratory fitness is an important factor in the risk of developing metabolic syndrome.
cardiorespiratory fitness and moderate alcohol consumption have a synergistic association with the incidence of metabolic syndrome.
